metadata.note: The Union Pacific's water-level answer to the Northern Pacific at Lewiston. Where the NP had to drop ~1,800 ft off the Palouse to get in (np_moscow_lewiston.geojson), the Oregon, Washington and Idaho Railroad -- incorporated in Oregon on August 8 1903 as a UP operating subsidiary -- simply followed the right (north) bank of the Snake River for 72.03 miles from Riparia, Washington up to Lewiston, and began operating on July 7 1908. Riparia connected onward to the OR&N system, and from 1908 Walla Walla and Lewiston were physically on the same railroad. But they were never joined by a through passenger train, and that was deliberate: the OR&N's Snake River Valley Railroad (Wallula-Grange City, opened December 1 1899) had been built precisely to give 'a better route to Spokane than the existing line via Walla Walla', so the through corridor bypassed Walla Walla nine years BEFORE the Lewiston line opened. Every documented through passenger working reflects that -- see 'passenger_service' below. Rather than keep duplicating each other into Lewiston, the UP and NP compromised: from December 3 1909 the jointly-owned Camas Prairie Railroad operated this line as part of a through route from Riparia to Grangeville, and kept operating it after the property passed to the Oregon-Washington Railroad and Navigation Company in December 1910.

geometry_sources: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap (Overpass), shortest rail path from Riparia to Lewiston over the surviving Snake River line (OSM 'Riparia Subdivision' / Camas Prairie trackage). 828 points, 114.43 km / 71.11 mi, with NO bridged gaps -- the whole route matched to connected track. That 71.11 mi against the documented 72.03 mi is a close match, so the modern alignment is taken to be the 1908 one.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: All frequencies here are estimates, not timetables, except where the 1920 and 1954 workings quoted under 'passenger_service' apply. Also unsourced: running times, and the exact construction start date (the Nez Perce County Museum says the UP 'completed its line to Riparia and up the Snake River into Lewiston in 1905', three years before the sourced July 7 1908 opening; that discrepancy is unresolved). The connecting Wallula-Grange City trackage (Snake River Valley Railroad, 1899) is now sourced AND drawn, in snake_river_valley_wallula_riparia.geojson, so the physical chain Walla Walla-Wallula-Riparia-Lewiston is visible for 1908-1910 (the Walla Walla features end in 1910). However, the older pre-1899 OR&N route that did run via Walla Walla and Starbuck is undrawn and only weakly sourced -- one search result dates a Walla Walla-Starbuck line to 1881 and Starbuck is documented as 'originally a junction on the main line of the Oregon Railroad and Navigation Company', but no reliable segment-by-segment source for it has been found.
metadata.passenger_service: CHECKED, and the answer is no: no through passenger service ever ran between Walla Walla and Lewiston. Walla Walla does not appear anywhere in the Camas Prairie passenger schedules. What actually ran: (1) 1920 -- Camas Prairie trains No. 5 and No. 6 worked Lewiston-Riparia and back (No. 5 dep Lewiston 7:20 PM, arr Riparia 10:05 PM; No. 6 dep Riparia 4:40 AM, arr Lewiston 7:10 AM, effective October 24 1920). (2) July 1954 -- trains 73/74 ran Ayer-Lewiston, calling at Tucannon, Riparia, Central Ferry, Penawawa, Swift, Almota, Wawawai, Crum, Bishop, Indian, Moses and Wilma. No Walla Walla. (3) The through Portland-Lewiston coach-sleeping car (8-Section) rode UP trains 20 and 19 on the Columbia River main line and was switched at AYER, not at Walla Walla, which sat on a branch off Wallula. A Walla Walla passenger bound for Lewiston therefore had to change trains. Camas Prairie passenger service ended between July 1957 and November 1958.

segments.note: From December 3 1909 the Camas Prairie Railroad -- owned jointly by the Northern Pacific and the Union Pacific's OR&N -- operated this line as part of a through route from Riparia to Grangeville. It was the settlement of the Harriman-Hill railroad war in north central Idaho: rather than each build its own duplicate network, the two systems shared one. Camas Prairie stayed the operating agent after the property passed to the Oregon-Washington Railroad and Navigation Company in December 1910, and ran until 1998, after which the corridor continued under short-line operation. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
